title: Given that every perfection is of God's essence, does personal subsistence follow; and is God, as communicable to three, a person (Cajetan)
pass_a_gloss: Article VIII. Given every perfection is of Gods essence, does personal subsistence follow from that; and is God as communicable to the three persons a person, as Cajetan held. §1: From prior doctrine a hard difficulty arises: if every perfection is of Gods essence, personal subsistence seems included → God common to three is a suppositum/person (subsistence = substantial perfection; suppositum has a more perfect mode of existing than the nature in it). Two questions: (1) is personal subsistence of Gods essence? (2) is God as God a person common to the whole Trinity? §2: Two observations before assertions. (Obs1) Philosophers take subsist three ways (Art. IV): not in a subject of inherence; not depending for the act of existing on that in which they are; not able to be in another suppositum. (Obs2) A fourth sense can be added: existing with no dependence on any creating/conserving cause — Gods proper, incommunicable, most perfect mode. §3 Assert1: Subsistence in senses 1–2 is essential to God and common to the Trinity (as actually existing is). §4 Assert2: Sense-3 subsistence, though in God it does not really differ from essence, is not truly of Gods essence — else God as God would be a person, and the three as one true God one person: absurd vs faith. §5 Assert3: Sense-4 subsistence (aseity) is of Gods essence / essential attribute. §6 Assert4: Distinguish perfectio: (A) negation imports imperfection (exist, live, Spirit, good, just); (B) negation does not (decrees of creation/governance; walking/speaking as human acts). §7: All A-genus perfections are of Gods essence necessarily; B-genus not (else decrees would be necessary and freedom of divine decrees lost). Personal subsistence referred to B-genus: its negation imperfects finite essence but not Deity, because divine essence includes a more perfect mode (aseity) than personal subsistence (communicable to men and angels). Finite essence lacks both existence-act and any mode more perfect than personality. §8: Suarez Trin. 3.10 has another (obscurer) perfection distinction — skipped; note his addendum: divinity prescinding from personal relations does not formally include their perfections but eminently (for infinity; Deity as root/foundation). §9: Second question easy once first solved: God as common to three is not a person. Cajetan: may be called persona completa if not persona stricte. Reply with Fonseca: avoid novel unused locutions alien to the Fathers; hearers may think three persons are one person/suppositum.
pass_b_english: Article VIII. This being laid down — that every perfection is of the essence of God — whether it follows that personal subsistence is of his essence; and whether God, insofar as he is communicable to the three persons of the Trinity, is a person, as Cajetan maintains.

1. From the preceding doctrine there arises a difficulty of no small weight concerning subsistence or personality: for since it has been established that every perfection is of the essence of God, it seems necessarily to follow that subsistence, or personality, is included in his essence; and therefore that God, insofar as he is common to the three persons of the Trinity, is a suppositum or person. The reason of the connection is this: because subsistence is a certain substantial perfection, and that not a slight one; for every suppositum has a more perfect mode of existing than the nature which exists in the suppositum. Here, therefore, two things are to be discussed: first, whether personal subsistence is of the essence of God; second, whether God, as God, is a certain person common to the whole Trinity.

2. That the former difficulty may be removed, after two observations have been set down beforehand, I will propose my sentence in several assertions. First it is to be held that subsistence is taken by the philosophers in three ways, as was said above: for (1) those things are said to subsist which do not exist in a subject of inherence; (2) those which do not so inexist that they depend, as to the act of existing, upon those in which they inexist; (3) those which in no way inexist in another suppositum, or can inexist in one. Second it is to be held that to these three significations of this word a fourth can be added, which, although it is less frequent, is nevertheless no less proper. For that being can be said to subsist which so exists that it depends in its being upon no creating or conserving cause: this mode of existing is proper to God, and cannot be communicated to any created being; and therefore it is without doubt the most perfect mode of existing.

3. These things being laid down, let this be Assertion 1. Subsistence taken in the first and second way is essential to God, and equally common to the Trinity: for just as it belongs essentially to God to exist in act, so also it is of the essence of God so to exist that he neither exists in any subject, nor depends, as to the act of existing, upon that suppositum in which he is.

4. Second Assertion. Subsistence taken in the third way, although insofar as it is in God it does not differ in the thing from his essence, nevertheless cannot truly be said to be of the essence of God: for whatever is of the essence of God belongs to God as God. If therefore personality is of the essence of God, God insofar as he is God is a person, and consequently all three persons, insofar as they are one true God, can truly be called one person: which is plainly absurd, and contrary to the principles of our faith.

5. Assertion 3. Subsistence taken in the fourth way is of the essence of God, or is an essential attribute of his: for to be the first Being, having its being from itself and not from elsewhere, is the very nature or essence of God.

6. Assertion 4. This word "perfection" is to be distinguished; for some are perfections whose negation imports imperfection — as to be or to exist, to live, to be a Spirit, to be good, to be just: for their opposites, namely not to exist, not to live, and so on, are manifestly imperfections. Others are perfections whose negation imports no imperfection: thus the most wise decrees of God concerning the creation and governance of things are perfections, but their negation imports no imperfection: for even if God had had no such decrees, indeed even if he had had decrees contrary to these, he would not have been more imperfect. So to walk, to run, to sit, to speak are perfections of a human being — for they are acts, and every act is a perfection: but the negation of those acts involves no imperfection; although the negation of the potencies from which they arise brands the thing to which it is attributed with a mark of imperfection. I say that the negation of these acts involves no imperfection, because a human being is not more imperfect when he does not walk than when he walks, or when he does not speak than when he speaks.

7. All perfections of the former kind are of the essence of God, and necessarily belong to him as God: but concerning perfections of the second order one must think otherwise; for they are not of the essence of God, nor do they necessarily belong to him as God — for example, the decrees of God concerning the eternal salvation and death of human beings, although they do not differ in the thing from his essence, are nevertheless not truly said to be of the essence of God: for if that were true, they would be in God by the necessity of nature, and thus the liberty of the divine decrees would be taken away. To this latter genus of perfections we refer personal subsistence; for although its negation, when it is attributed to the finite essence of creatures, involves imperfection, yet when it is attributed to the Godhead, or to the divine nature, it imports no blot of imperfection. The reason of the disparity is this: the divine essence includes in itself a certain mode of existing far more perfect than personal subsistence — namely the mode of existing without dependence in being upon any creating or conserving cause. I say that this mode of existing is more perfect than personal subsistence, because in it is placed the perfection of the first being; and on that account it cannot be communicated to creatures: but personal subsistence is communicated both to human beings and to angels. On the contrary, the finite essence of creatures includes in itself neither the act of existing, nor any mode of existing more perfect than personality: and therefore it is imperfect on account of the defect of personality, whereas the Godhead is in no way imperfect on account of the lack of such subsistence.

8. Francisco Suárez, On the Trinity book 3, chapter 10, brings forward another distinction of perfection; but a more obscure and difficult one, and therefore I will not propose it here. But this is carefully to be noted which he adds to that distinction — namely, that divinity, the personal relations or subsistences being prescinded, does not formally include their perfections; yet it includes them eminently, both because this is necessary for the infinity of that being, and because the Godhead itself is the root and foundation of all those perfections.

9. The latter question is easily solved once the former difficulty has been removed: for since that subsistence which is proper to supposita does not belong to God as he is common to the three persons, it is to be said without fear that God so considered is not a person. But (says Cajetan) God, insofar as he is common to the three persons, although he is not a person strictly and properly speaking, can nevertheless be called a complete person. I answer with Fonseca that in divine things novel and unused locutions, abhorrent from every custom of the Fathers, are not to be employed — especially since someone can be deceived by such a manner of speaking and suppose that the three persons are one person, or one suppositum.
source_text:
ART. VIII.
An hoc posito, quod omnis perfectio sit de essentia Dei, sequatur subsistentiam personalem esse de ejus essentia: et an Deus, quatenus est communicabilis tribus personis Trinitatis, sit persona, ut statuit Cajetanus.

1. Ex praecedente doctrina, non levis oritur difficultas de subsistentia seu personalitate: cum enim statutum sit, omnem perfectionem esse de essentia Dei, necessario sequi videtur subsistentiam, seu personalitatem in ejus essentia includi; ideoque Deum, quatenus est communis tribus personis Trinitatis, esse suppositum aut personam: ratio connexionis est; quia subsistentia est perfectio quaedam substantialis, eaque non exigua; suppositum enim omne perfectiorem habet modum existendi, quam natura quae in supposito existit. Hic igitur duo discutienda sunt: primo, an subsistentia personalis sit de essentia Dei: secundo, an Deus qua Deus, sit persona quaedam toti Trinitati communis.

2. Ut prior difficultas tollatur, praemissis duabus observationibus, meam sententiam aliquot assertionibus proponam; primo tenendum est: subsistentiam tribus modis accipi a Philosophis, ut supra dictum est: 1. enim ea subsistere dicuntur, quae non existunt in subjecto inhaesionis: 2. ea quae non ita insunt, ut ab iis in quibus insunt, quoad existendi actum pendeant: 3. ea quae nullo modo alteri supposito insunt, aut inesse possunt. Secundo tenendum est, tribus his significationibus hujus vocis, addi posse quartam, quae licet minus frequens sit, non minus tamen propria est. Illud enim Ens dici potest subsistere, quod ita existit ut a nulla causa procreante, aut conservante, in suo esse pendeat: hic modus existendi, Dei proprius est, nec ulli enti creato communicari potest; ideoque proculdubio perfectissimus modus existendi est.

3. His positis, haec sit Assert. 1. Subsistentia primo et secundo modo accepta, est DEO essentialis, aeque Trinitati communis: sicut enim essentialiter Deo competit actu existere, ita etiam est de essentia Dei sic existere, ut neque in aliquo subjecto existat, neque ab eo supposito in quo est, quoad actum existendi pendeat.

4. Secunda Assert. Subsistentia tertio modo accepta, etsi quatenus est in DEO, re non differat ab ejus essentia, non tamen vere dici potest esse de essentia DEI: quicquid enim est de essentia Dei, illud Deo, qua Deus est, competit. Si igitur personalitas est de essentia Dei, Deus quatenus est Deus, est persona, et per consequens, omnes tres personae, quatenus sunt unus verus DEUS, vere dici possunt una persona: quod sane absurdum est, et nostrae fidei principiis contrarium.

5. Assert. 3. Subsistentia quarto modo accepta, est de essentia DEI, seu est essentiale ejus attributum: nam esse primum Ens, a se et non aliunde suum esse habens, est ipsissima natura seu essentia DEI.

6. Assert. 4. Vocabulum hoc (perfectio) distinguendum est; aliae enim sunt perfectiones, quarum negatio imperfectionem importat, ut esse seu existere, vivere, esse Spiritum, esse bonum, esse justum: horum enim opposita, nimirum non existere, non vivere, etc. manifeste imperfectiones sunt. Aliae sunt perfectiones, quarum negatio nullam imperfectionem importat: sic sapientissima DEI decreta de creatione et gubernatione rerum, perfectiones sunt, sed eorum negatio nullam imperfectionem importat: quamvis enim DEUS nulla talia decreta habuisset, imo quamvis contraria his decreta habuisset, imperfectior non fuisset: sic ambulare, currere, sedere, loqui, sunt perfectiones hominis, sunt enim actus, omnisque actus est perfectio: at negatio horum actuum nullam imperfectionem involvit; quamvis negatio potentiarum ex quibus oriuntur, imperfectionis notam rei, cui tribuitur, inurat: dico negationem horum actuum nullam imperfectionem involvere; quia homo non est imperfectior cum non ambulat, quam cum ambulat, aut cum non loquitur, quam cum loquitur.

7. Prioris generis perfectiones omnes sunt de essentia DEI, illique, qua DEUS est, necessario conveniunt: at de perfectionibus secundi ordinis, aliter sentiendum est; non enim sunt de essentia DEI, nec illi necessario conveniunt, qua DEUS est, v.g. decreta DEI de hominum aeterna salute et morte, etsi re non differant ab ejus essentia, non tamen vere dicuntur esse de essentia DEI: si enim hoc esset verum, ex necessitate naturae DEO inessent, et sic libertas decretorum divinorum tolleretur. Ad posterius genus perfectionum, subsistentiam personalem referimus; etsi enim ejus negatio, cum essentiae finitae creaturarum tribuitur, imperfectionem involvat; cum tamen Deitati, seu naturae divinae attribuitur, nullam imperfectionis labem importat: ratio imparitatis est haec; essentia divina in se includit modum quendam existendi, longe perfectiorem subsistentia personali, nimirum modum existendi absque dependentia in essendo ab ulla causa procreante, aut conservante: dico hunc modum existendi esse perfectiorem subsistentia personali; quia in eo posita est perfectio primi entis; et ob id creaturis communicari nequit: subsistentia vero personalis et hominibus, et Angelis communicatur. Contra vero, essentia finita creaturarum in se neque existendi actum includit, neque ullum existendi modum personalitate perfectiorem: ideoque ea imperfecta est, ob defectum personalitatis, cum Deitas nullo modo imperfecta sit, ob carentiam talis subsistentiae.

8. Franciscus Suarez, lib. 3. de Trinit. Cap. 10, aliam distinctionem perfectionis affert; sed magis obscuram, et difficilem, ideoque eam hic non proponam: illud autem diligenter notandum est, quod isti distinctioni addit, videlicet, divinitatem, praecisis relationibus seu subsistentiis personalibus, non includere formaliter perfectiones earum: includere tamen illas eminenter, tum quia hoc necessarium est ad infinitatem illius entis; tum quia ipsa Deitas est radix, et fundamentum omnium illarum perfectionum.

9. Posterior quaestio facile solvitur, sublata priori difficultate: cum enim DEO, ut est communis tribus personis, ea subsistentia non conveniat, quae suppositorum est propria: intrepide dicendum est, DEUM sic consideratum non esse personam. At (inquit Cajetanus) DEUS quatenus est communis tribus personis, etsi non sit persona stricte et proprie loquendo, potest tamen dici persona completa. Respondeo cum Fonseca, in rebus divinis non usurpandas esse novas, et inusitatas locutiones, et ab omni Patrum consuetudine abhorrentes: praesertim cum quis decipi possit tali loquendi modo, et existimare tres personas esse unam personam, aut suppositum.
